intro: Well, so, anyway, I mean, mind you, the thing is… These small words carry almost no meaning, but they organise conversation, show your attitude and give you time to think. Used well, they make the difference between correct English and truly fluent English.
objectifs: Understand what discourse markers do: organise, rephrase, qualify and manage turns.
Use the essential markers with the right meaning: well, so, right, anyway, actually, I mean, mind you, then again.
React naturally as a listener (fair enough, I see, exactly, no way).
Replace fillers translated from your own language with real English equivalents.

texte: A discourse marker does not change the content of a sentence, but it tells the listener how to interpret it: “Well…” announces a qualified answer or a reservation, “Anyway…” brings the conversation back to the main topic, “Mind you…” adds a restriction.

They are not “mistakes” or hesitations to remove: native speakers use them all the time. The problem is overuse (“like” in every sentence) or misuse, when learners transfer the fillers of their first language.
They usually come at the start of an utterance, form their own short intonation group and are often followed by a tiny pause.
exemples: Well, it's not quite that simple.
“Well”: an answer with a reservation, not a simple yes.
Anyway, where was I? Oh yes, the budget.
“Anyway”: back to the topic after a digression.

sections.titre: Organising: opening, moving on, changing topic
texte: These markers structure the conversation like road signs. “Right” and “OK” open or close a stage; “so” introduces a conclusion or a new question; “by the way” starts a digression; “anyway” ends it.

lignes: open, move to the next stage
So, what did the doctor say?
By the way, did you get my email?
build on what was just said
Speaking of which, how's your new flat?
end the digression, return to the topic
As I was saying / Going back to…

exemples: Right, I think we've covered everything. Shall we stop there?

texte: When you are looking for words or want to be more exact, English uses “I mean”, “or rather”, “in other words”, “let me put it another way”.
“Actually” is mainly used to correct or politely contradict what was just said, or to give surprising information: “Actually, it was Tuesday, not Monday.” It is not a filler for every sentence.
“Sort of” and “kind of” soften a word (“it's sort of complicated”); very common in speech, best avoided in formal writing.
exemples: It was a good meeting. I mean, nothing was decided, but people talked.
“I mean” clarifies or qualifies what came before.
“You're from Lyon, right?” “Actually, I'm from Grenoble.”
It's kind of hard to explain.

texte: These markers show your position. “Mind you” (mainly BrE) adds a restriction to what you just said; “then again” gives the other side of the question; “still” keeps an idea in spite of everything; “after all” reminds people of an obvious reason.

“The thing is…” introduces the real problem; “to be honest / frankly” announces a direct opinion; “look” or “listen” at the start of a sentence signals firmness (even irritation), so use them carefully.

lignes: The hotel was great. Mind you, it was expensive.
give the other point of view
It's far. Then again, the trains are fast.
It rained all week. Still, we had fun.
Let him rest. After all, he's been ill.
I'd love to come. The thing is, I'm working.
To be honest, I didn't enjoy the film.
At the end of the day
what really matters in the end
At the end of the day, it's your decision.
Look, I understand, but we can't change it now.

exemples: The salary isn't great. Then again, the team is lovely.

texte: In English, listeners show they are following with short responses (backchannelling). Staying silent can seem cold or uninterested, especially on the phone.

Agreement: “Exactly.”, “Absolutely.”, “Fair enough.” (= that's reasonable, I accept it). Understanding: “I see.”, “Right.”, “Mm-hm.”. Surprise: “Really?”, “No way!” (informal), “You're joking!”. Sympathy: “Oh no.”, “That's a shame.”, “I know.”
exemples: “I can't come because my daughter's ill.” “Oh, fair enough.”

texte: Learners often translate the fillers of their first language word for word, which produces strange sentences. French speakers, for example, say “After, …” for “That said, …” or “Finally, …” for “I mean, …”. Learn the real English equivalents.

lignes: Then again / That said, it depends.
So there you go. / That's it, really.
a tag at the end of a sentence

formule: Marker at the start + tiny pause: organise (right, so, anyway) · rephrase (I mean, actually) · qualify (mind you, then again, still) · respond (fair enough, I see)
prononciation: Hesitant “Well” is often lengthened with a fall-rise: “We-ell…”; it signals a reservation.
“So” to restart is light and short; “So?” alone with a rise means “And what of it?”, which can sound rude.
“Actually” often reduces to /ˈæktʃli/ (three syllables instead of four) in fast speech.
Opening “Right” falls firmly; “…, right?” rising at the end asks for confirmation.
“Fair enough”: stress on “nough” /feər ɪˈnʌf/, falling tone.
erreurs: After, it depends on the price.
Then again / That said, it depends on the price.
“After” is not a discourse marker for “that said”.
In fact, I went to the shop. In fact, it was closed.
I went to the shop, but it was actually closed.
“Actually” highlights unexpected information; don't repeat “in fact”.
Finally, I mean, it wasn't bad.
Well, I mean, it wasn't bad.
“Finally” means “at the end”, not “what I mean is”.
Good, let's start.
Right, let's start. / OK, let's start.
To organise, use right / OK.
It was expensive, voilà.
It was expensive, you know. / So there you go.
“Voilà” at the end is not natural in English.
Eventually, by the way, we need to finish the report.
Anyway, we need to finish the report.
To return to the main topic: anyway.
Like, I was, like, so tired, like.
I was so tired.
Repeated “like” is very informal and irritating outside casual chat.

dialogue.contexte: Two colleagues chat during a coffee break at a company in Quebec City.
lignes: So, how was the conference in Halifax?
Well, the talks were interesting. Mind you, the hotel was miles from the venue.
A positive answer with a reservation.
Oh no. Did you have to take taxis?
Actually, there was a shuttle. By the way, I met your old manager there.
No way! Speaking of which, is she still at the bank?
Surprise, then building on the topic.
She's left, actually. Anyway, the thing is, they've offered me a job.
Back to the main news, and the real point.
Really? Are you going to take it?
I don't know. The salary's better. Then again, I'd have to move.
Fair enough. At the end of the day, it's your call.
Acceptance and what matters in the end.

mots: Anyway, let's get back to the plan.
used to return to the main topic
It's small. Mind you, it's cheap.
It's risky. Then again, it could pay off.
used to introduce a new topic
Incidentally, the office is closed on Friday.
The thing is, I don't have a car.
used to introduce the real problem

exercices.consigne: Give the function of the marker: return to the topic, correct, add a reservation, give the other point of view.
items: Anyway, as I was saying, the deadline is Friday.
return to the topic
Actually, the meeting is at ten, not nine.
correct
The flat is lovely. Mind you, it's noisy.
add a reservation
It's a long trip. Then again, the scenery is amazing.
give the other point of view

exercices.consigne: Complete with: by the way, after all, the thing is, still, fair enough, I mean.
items: I'd love to help. ___, I'm away that weekend.
The thing is
“I can't come, I'm ill.” “Oh, ___.”
fair enough
Don't be too hard on him. ___, it's his first week.
After all
It was a difficult year. ___, we finished the project.
Still
___, have you seen my keys?
By the way
The film was fine. ___, it wasn't brilliant, but I enjoyed it.
I mean
“We've won the contract!”
Really? That's fantastic! / No way! Brilliant!
“I can't stay late, I have to pick up my son.”
Fair enough. / Of course, no problem.
“My flight was cancelled.”
Oh no! That's a shame. / Oh no, what happened?
After, it's your choice.
Then again / That said, it's your choice.
Good, let's begin the meeting.
Right / OK, let's begin the meeting.
The train was late, so of the blow I missed my interview.
The train was late, so I missed my interview.

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence, starting with a suitable marker.
items: Let's stop talking about this; see you tomorrow.
Anyway, see you tomorrow.
The real problem is that I don't have time.
The thing is, I don't have time.
On the other hand, the price is reasonable. (use a spoken marker)
Then again, the price is reasonable.

exercices.consigne: Write a short exchange (5–6 lines) in which you tell a friend some news. Use at least five different markers.
items: Example answer

A: So, guess what? I've been offered a place at the University of Montreal. B: No way! That's amazing! A: Well, it's not all good news. The thing is, there's no scholarship. B: Oh, I see. Then again, you could work part-time. A: True. Mind you, rent there isn't cheap. Anyway, I'll decide next week.

a_retenir: Markers organise (right, so, by the way, anyway), rephrase (I mean, actually), qualify (mind you, then again, still, after all) and show listening (fair enough, I see).
“Actually” corrects or surprises; it is not a filler for every sentence.
They come first, followed by a tiny pause; in formal writing, replace them with real linkers (however, in addition).
Don't translate your own fillers: “that said” = then again, not “after”; “I mean”, not “finally”.
